payload.name: maximum-flow-derivative
payload.scope: A human-made voice-quality parameter quantifying the peak rate of change of glottal flow within the glottal cycle, built to persist as a standardized clinical measure of glottal dynamics and voice-disorder assessment in laryngology and speech-language pathology.

payload.body: The maximum flow derivative (MFD) is a voice-quality parameter quantifying the peak rate of change of glottal flow within a glottal cycle, reported per cycle and aggregated over voiced frames. Given the glottal flow waveform g(n) and the fundamental period T0 from pitch tracking, MFD is computed as the maximum magnitude of the first derivative (or first difference) of g within each pitch-synchronous cycle, max |g(n+1) - g(n)|, then aggregated across cycles by the median or mean over the analyzed frames. Its parameters are: (1) the glottal flow waveform g(n) — the inverse-filtering estimate of the glottal source, (2) the fundamental period T0 from pitch tracking, which frames the per-cycle window, (3) the derivative operator — first difference or finite difference over the sampled flow, (4) the normalization choice — absolute units (volume per sample interval) or relative to the cycle's maximum flow, and (5) the cross-cycle aggregation (median or mean). A high MFD marks a sharp glottal closure (pressed, spiky phonation) and a low MFD marks a gradual closure (breathy phonation), with maintained reference ranges separating typical from disordered phonation. It is reported in standardized units and persists as a member of the voice-quality measurement map: implemented in voice-analysis toolkits (Praat, laryngology suites), documented in laryngology and speech-language pathology, and maintained alongside jitter, shimmer, and the phase quotients. [formal: derivatio fluminis maxima | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

payload.name: formant-dispersion
payload.scope: A human-made voice-quality parameter quantifying the mean spacing between the first three formant frequencies of a voiced speech segment, built to persist as a standardized clinical measure of vocal-tract length and voice characterization in laryngology and speech science.

payload.name: formant-dispersion
payload.scope: A human-made voice-quality parameter quantifying the mean spacing between the first three formant frequencies of a voiced speech segment, built to persist as a standardized clinical measure of vocal-tract length and voice characterization in laryngology and speech science.

payload.body: Formant dispersion (D) is a voice-quality parameter quantifying the mean spacing between the first three formant frequencies of a voiced segment, reported in hertz as D = (F3 - F1) / 2, equivalently the mean of (F2 - F1) and (F3 - F2). Given formant estimates F1, F2, F3 per analysis frame, D is computed per frame from the frame's three lowest formant frequencies and aggregated across the voiced segment by mean (and, where maintained, standard deviation). Its parameters are: (1) the formant frequency estimates F1, F2, F3 per analysis frame — the vocal-tract resonances located by formant tracking, (2) the dispersion operator — (F3 - F1)/2 or the mean of consecutive spacings, (3) the cross-frame aggregation (mean, standard deviation, or median) over the analyzed voiced segment. A larger dispersion indicates a shorter, stiffer vocal tract (child-like or laryngectomized voice) and a smaller dispersion a longer tract, with maintained reference ranges separating typical from disordered phonation. It is reported in hertz and persists as a member of the voice-quality measurement map: implemented in voice-analysis toolkits, documented in laryngology and speech-language pathology, and maintained alongside jitter, shimmer, the phase quotients, and the noise ratios. [formal: diffusio formantorum | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

payload.name: peak-flow

payload.name: peak-flow
payload.scope: A human-made voice-quality parameter quantifying the peak glottal flow within each glottal cycle, built to persist as a standardized clinical measure of glottal source dynamics and voice-disorder assessment in laryngology and speech-language pathology.

payload.body: Peak flow is a voice-quality parameter quantifying the peak glottal flow within each glottal cycle, reported per cycle and aggregated over voiced frames. Given the glottal flow waveform g(n) and the fundamental period T0 from pitch tracking, the peak flow is computed as the maximum of g within each pitch-synchronous cycle, max_n g(n), then aggregated across cycles by the median or mean over the analyzed frames. Its parameters are: (1) the glottal flow waveform g(n) — the inverse-filtering estimate of the glottal source, (2) the fundamental period T0 from pitch tracking, which frames the per-cycle window, (3) the peak operator — the maximum of the sampled flow within the cycle, (4) the normalization choice — absolute flow units or relative to the cycle's mean flow, and (5) the cross-cycle aggregation (median or mean). A high peak flow marks a leaky, breathy source with a large open-phase flow excursion and a low peak flow a pressed source with a tightly modulated pulse, with maintained reference ranges separating typical from disordered phonation. It is reported in standardized units and persists as a member of the voice-quality measurement map: implemented in voice-analysis toolkits, documented in laryngology and speech-language pathology, and maintained alongside the maximum flow derivative, voice onset time, jitter, shimmer, and the phase quotients. [formal: flumen summitum | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

payload.body: The glottal closure instant (GCI) is a voice-quality parameter locating the point of glottal closure within each glottal cycle: the instant at which the glottal airflow returns to baseline and the closed phase begins. In the pinned sense it is estimated from the glottal flow waveform (glottogram) g(n) and the fundamental period T0 from pitch tracking: within each pitch-synchronous cycle, the GCI is the time point of the cycle's minimum glottal flow - the flow trough returning to baseline - equivalently the point where the first derivative of the flow crosses zero from negative to positive. It is reported per cycle as a time point and as the normalized GCI (nGCI), the difference between successive closure instants divided by the intervening fundamental period, a dimensionless ratio with maintained reference ranges separating typical from disordered phonation: a prolonged nGCI marks increased glottal closure as in spastic or hyperfunctional dysphonia, a shortened nGCI a breathy, insufficiently closed source. Parameters: (1) the glottal flow waveform g(n) - the inverse-filtering estimate of the glottal source, (2) the fundamental period T0 from pitch tracking, which frames the per-cycle window, (3) the closure operator - the flow-minimum location, the first-derivative zero crossing from negative to positive within the cycle, (4) the normalized reporting - nGCI as a dimensionless ratio, (5) the cross-cycle aggregation (median or mean over the analyzed frames). It is reported in standardized units and persists as a maintained member of the voice-quality measurement map: implemented in voice-analysis toolkits, documented in laryngology and speech-language pathology, and maintained alongside the closure quotient, the open quotient, the maximum flow derivative, and the return phase. [formal: instant clausurae glottidis | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

payload.reasoning: Removal test fails (Law 8b). Phonation is the physiological process: its operating inputs are parameters (1)-(2), subglottal pressure P(t) and vocal-fold contact area A(t), which generate the glottal flow g(t). T0 is a property of the periodic output, not an operand of the process — the folds vibrate at T0 whether or not anyone measures it, and removing pitch tracking changes nothing about the process's operating: the period still exists and is measurable by EGG or stroboscopy. The note confuses a measurement route for a property with an operational dependency: pitch tracking READS the process's periodicity; the process does not consume the estimator. The accepted family pattern (closure-quotient, HNR → pitch-tracking) holds because those are per-cycle computations that TAKE T0 as an input operand; phonation produces the periodicity rather than consuming it. The dependency, if any, runs the other direction.

payload.name: glottal-source-spectral-tilt
payload.scope: A human-made voice-quality measurement parameter quantifying the slope of the glottal source spectrum (spectral tilt of the glottal flow waveform), built to persist as a standardized clinical parameter in speech science and laryngology.

payload.body: The glottal source spectral tilt (GSS) is a voice-quality parameter quantifying the slope of the glottal source spectrum: the linear-regression slope of the log power spectrum of the glottal flow waveform g(n) versus log frequency, reported in dB/octave. From the frame-aligned glottal-flow waveform g(n) (glottogram), the per-frame power spectrum of g is estimated, the log-log regression of log PSD against log frequency is fitted over the regression band (classically 100-4000 Hz), and the slope is the source spectral tilt for that frame; frames are aggregated by median or mean over the analyzed voiced frames. Its parameters are: (1) the glottal flow waveform g(n) - the inverse-filtering estimate of the glottal source, the sole operand, (2) the per-frame power-spectrum estimate of g (window, smoothing), (3) the regression band (classically 100-4000 Hz), (4) the regression method - log-log linear fit of the source PSD, and (5) the cross-frame aggregation (median or mean). A steeper negative tilt marks a bright, pressed source with strong high-frequency source energy; a flatter tilt marks a breathy, energy-decaying source, with maintained reference ranges separating typical from disordered phonation. It is reported in standardized units (dB/octave) and persists as a member of the voice-quality measurement map: implemented in voice-analysis toolkits, documented in laryngology and speech-language pathology (the Dewaele glottal-source parameter set), and maintained alongside the maximum flow derivative, the harmonicity, jitter, shimmer, and the phase quotients. payload.body: The glottal source spectrum is the per-frame power spectrum of the glottal flow waveform g(n) (the glottogram): the spectral representation of the estimated glottal source over each voiced frame. Given the frame-aligned glottal-flow waveform g(n) - the inverse-filtering estimate of the glottal source - the glottal source spectrum for a frame is the power spectrum of g over that frame, typically the squared magnitude of the frame's discrete Fourier transform |G(f)|^2 (or its Welch/averaged estimate), expressed in dB and reported across the source-relevant band (classically 100-4000 Hz). Its parameters are: (1) the glottal flow waveform g(n) - the inverse-filtering estimate of the glottal source, the sole operand, (2) the per-frame spectral estimate (window, overlap, averaging method), and (3) the reporting band and units (dB, the source-relevant frequency range). The source spectrum is a maintained diagnostic representation in its own right: its overall shape - the balance of energy between low and high frequencies - characterizes the glottal source and is read clinically (a steeply falling source spectrum marks a breathy, energy-decaying source; a flatter or high-frequency-forward source spectrum a bright, pressed source), and it is the operand from which the source-domain voice-quality measures (the glottal source spectral tilt, the source harmonicity, the glottal-to-noise ratio) are computed. It is reported in standardized units and persists as a maintained source-domain representation in voice-analysis toolkits and laryngology, implemented alongside the glottogram and the source parameters. [formal: spectrum fontis glottis | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

payload.body: The source harmonicity is a voice-quality parameter quantifying the balance between the periodic (harmonic) and the aperiodic (noise-like) components of the glottal source. It is computed from the glottal source spectrum - the per-frame power spectrum of the glottal-flow waveform g(n) (the glottogram) - which is the sole operand: the harmonic energy is measured over the frequency bands at the fundamental f0 and its integer harmonics, the aperiodic energy over the inter-harmonic regions, and the ratio is formed over the source-relevant band. Parameters: (1) the glottal source spectrum - the per-frame power spectrum of g(n), the sole operand, (2) the fundamental-frequency estimate f0 locating the harmonic comb, (3) the number of harmonics covered and the band widths around each harmonic, and (4) the ratio form of the measure, E_harmonic / (E_harmonic + E_aperiodic), a value in [0, 1]. A high value marks a dominantly periodic (modal) source and a low value an aperiodic (breathy, harsh, or dysphonic) source; it is reported as a dimensionless ratio with maintained reference ranges separating typical from disordered phonation. Persistence mechanism: a standardized clinical parameter of the glottal source parameter set, implemented in voice-analysis toolkits (Praat, laryngology suites), documented in laryngology and speech-language pathology, and maintained alongside the glottal source spectral tilt, the glottal-to-noise ratio, the maximum flow derivative, jitter, and shimmer as a member of the voice-quality measurement map.
